Look at this line and this one. This is me talking, my real stories, my real numbers, the way I write.

keeps.text: Back in 2021, I used to pay around $150 to $300 per one technical guide like this one. And sometimes I needed to wait like 7 days to finish it because It requires a lot of experiments, a lot of tests, back and forth between me and the writer. Then in 2022, one year later, I published a video here on my channel showing you how to write a full blog post in 10 minutes with the help of AI. Around 300,000 people watched the video.

And it was really fast, yes. But I warned you then in that video. To use AI as writing assistant and don't just copy and paste because it wrote generic content. Today we have a name for that content, AI slop, and we don't want that. So today, with the new AI-powered content factory I built,
and you will see today, honestly, no writer I ever hired
could do the experiments and tests
and write like this system. Sorry writers, but this is reality
and you should adapt.

You'll have a complete mind shift. WinCoding and Building with AI. It's free, grab it, and let's continue our work.

keeps.text: Okay, so here's the input. One simple prompt
self-host Supabase, focus on the hard parts nobody documents, and run it on a real server. That's it. No prompt engineering, no outline, nothing.

The contract, which is the first step in the content factory system, already knows all the stages. So the first thing it does, it doesn't write, it reads. It pulls real search data, fetches the top-ranking results on Google, and reads every single one. What they cover, what they miss,

and look at this, really super interesting. I told it to target self-host Supabase, and it has around 740 searches per month. It came back and said people actually search Supabase self-host, and the full cluster is around 1,100 searches a month. 3 times bigger than what I thought. This is the importance of relying on real data when writing. And the system is really honest. I built it in a way if it can't really find a real gap that we can fill online, it just tell me the topic is weak before anything written, so we don't waste time on a topic That's not useful and nobody will benefit from. So some ideas just die at step 1, and that's a feature.

keeps.text: if it passes, then it writes a plan. The main idea, the 8 experiments it wants to run, and the cost. In my case, around $0.70, and with a hard cap of $1.50, it cannot pass. And then it stops. It doesn't touch any server before I approve the plan and the budget.
I approve, and now the fun part. The AI, the engine, will rent a server. In my case, I'm using DigitalOcean. They have simple API access and fast server creation process, so I use it as my lab.
It cloned the stack in 2 seconds, pulled like 8.9 gigabytes of images in 114 seconds, and 20 seconds later,
Supabase was up. 11 containers, all healthy, on a 4 gigabyte box. And it measured everything.
down to the RAM of every container.

Then it starts breaking things on purpose. And this is where it becomes really interesting because failures are evidence too. And here where it's really super difficult and takes a lot of time for you as a writer to do these experiments,

while AI can run these experiments in like a couple of minutes. Then the big one. It rotated security keys and the connection pooler silently died. No errors, clients just hang forever. One experiment was stuck for 8 hours because of this. It diagnosed it, fixed it, and documented it. The fix became the headline advice of the guide: set all your secrets before the first boot, or your pool dies quietly later. No guy drinking on Google knows this. My factory system knows it because it lived it. It experimented it, and when the experiment finishes, it destroys the server.
The teardown is part of the work, and the total bill is like 35 cents.

keeps.text: Now of course a guide like this requires screenshots, and this is the most boring part for writers, especially technical guides where we need a lot of screenshots. The system I built takes them by itself. It drives a real browser Using Playwright— we talked about this before— it logs into the app we deployed and shoots every screenshot the guide needs. Think about how much time this is saving you.
and it really has one rule I love.
it never blurs a secret. If a real key appears on the screen, it replaces it automatically with a fake one.

keeps.text: After all this, it finally writes.

but before drafting, it pulls up my brain, my voice rules, my beliefs, my beliefs about self-hosting, The real story of my cloud bills and how I saved $8,000 a year, and the reason why I moved to self-hosting. So the draft opens with my argument. It's me talking, my brain talking. In my words, in my voice,
and backed by its evidence.
Now after the draft, we have the verification loops, and this is super important. One loop checks the evidence.

and one attacks the draft trying to find a wrong claim. One checks my voice, and each loop runs until it comes back clean. Then it ships. The page gets built, checked, rendered, and committed to my site's repo.

But there is one more thing before it goes live, and this is the most important step in the whole flow. It is the same rule from 2022. I read the full guide again, word by word, myself. Not skimming, really reading. Every claim, every command, every number. You never just copy and paste or rely directly on the output.

Now compared to 2022, now the AI does 1,000 times more of the work and the rule did not move. Nothing goes out under my name before I read and verify and approve. So automate the work as much as you can, but never automate the responsibility.

keeps.text: Now the last part, and my favorite one.

Look at the first stage of the pipeline and the last one. The first thing it does, it reads my brain. And the last thing it does, it feeds my brain again. Every lesson from the lab, every experiment, every result gets distilled and offered back to the brain, and I approve what it enters. So every guide makes my brain better, and a better brain makes the next guide better. It's a closed loop, and this is why exactly The brain video came first last week. If you missed it, you'll find the link in the description below. Go watch it and see how you can build your own brain and connect with AI.
if you learned something new today, smash the like button

And if you find any AI slop, tell me in the comments. I read every one of them. Thank you and see you in the upcoming videos.
